docs.title: Optimal 3D Trajectory Planning for a Fixed-Wing UAV
docs.text:
Four missions planned around no-fly zones and through waypoints, then flown by a point-mass and a 6-DoF model of a generic UAV, using the public code. The dotted straight line is what a cold start would try: it crosses the zones.

Documentation of a Bachelor's thesis (UPC – ESEIAAT) carried out with CIMNE and in collaboration with Singular Aircraft: a 3D trajectory optimiser for the amphibious heavy UAV Flyox I, built on trapezoidal direct collocation and IPOPT, and accelerated by a Hybrid A* warm-start chain.

docs.title: Missions around no-fly zones
docs.text:
A Hybrid A* planner finds a flyable path around the active no-fly zones and through the waypoints, and both aircraft models fly it in closed loop. All four missions use a generic UAV at 25 m/s with 30° of bank, which gives a planning turn radius of 143 m.

  • Every mission is flown clear of every zone. Every waypoint is passed well inside its tolerance.
  • The cold start would be infeasible. A straight line runs 200–394 m deep into a zone. This is why the thesis's cold-start solver failed in its no-fly-zone and waypoint scenarios (14. Warm-start benchmark).
  • These are flyable reference paths, not optima. They are the kind of warm start the thesis hands to its optimiser, and the optimiser is not part of the public code.

Each mission in detail: Worked examples → UC-07.

About the code

This work was designed exclusively as a product for Singular Aircraft. For privacy reasons towards the company, the full software repository cannot be shared. What can be shared is the knowledge: the research, the mathematical methods and their application in code. That is what these pages document, through equations, diagrams, pseudocode and results. The repository also includes a restricted public edition of the code (code/): a generic aircraft, the dynamic models, the collocation formulation, the planner and runnable examples. See Code: public edition.

flowchart LR

A cheap geometric search provides a path; inverse dynamics turns it into a dynamically plausible guess; a fast point-mass optimisation refines it; a projection seeds the full 6-DoF optimisation. Each step hands the next one a better starting point, which is what makes the interior-point solver converge reliably. The missions above show the first step (the path) working with the public code.

docs.title: 1. Problem and requirements
docs.text:
TL;DR

Build a 3D trajectory solver for a Mission Management System (MMS) that plans accelerated climb/cruise/descent profiles, respects terrain and no-fly zones, and answers in under 4 seconds.

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text: A flight plan for a small aircraft is usually a polyline of waypoints flown at constant speed. That is easy to compute but wasteful: a real aircraft accelerates in the climb, trades altitude for speed, and banks to turn. Taking this into account yields trajectories that are faster or burn less fuel, but turns the planning problem into a large nonlinear optimisation. If, in addition, the aircraft detects a restricted zone in flight, a new trajectory has to be produced quickly.

docs.title: Reference platform
docs.text: Flyox I (Singular Aircraft): amphibious heavy UAV, MTOW 1,850 kg, payload 850 kg, range 1,200 km. The aircraft used in the validation is the reference airframe MSN012, a full-scale implementation of the platform; its data are in the MSN012 appendix.

docs.title: Requirements (selected)
docs.text: Area Requirement Dynamics Coupled 6-DoF model that optimises controls and vehicle dynamics as one system; wind vector field supported Constraints Terrain (DEM), no-fly zones (NFZ), geofence, waypoints, actuator deflection limits Warm start Several strategies, selectable per use case; analytical seed (Dubins / straight segments) for recovery Transcription Independent of the solver: direct collocation and multiple shooting; Euler, RK4 and trapezoidal schemes Performance Feasible solution within 4.0 s per tactical look-ahead window; tolerance 1e-4 Interfaces JSON mission input; WGS-84 geodetic output for autopilots; native Linux SiL execution Safety Input range checks; fall back to last valid segment or analytical seed on timeout; log iterations and residuals

docs.title: Scope of the thesis
docs.text:
The thesis delivers the numerical core: two dynamic formulations, the NLP transcription, the constraint set, the cost function with regularisation, the warm-start chain, and a validation and benchmarking campaign. Closed-loop control, stochastic wind and multi-aircraft coordination are out of scope (see Conclusions).

docs.title: 2. State of the art
docs.text:
TL;DR

Graph planners are fast but ignore dynamics; numerical optimal control respects dynamics but is slow and fragile without a good initial guess. The gap this work addresses is the bridge between the two.

docs.title: Three families of methods
docs.text:
1. Geometric and graph-based planning (A*, Hybrid A*, RRT-like methods). They find collision-free paths quickly. Hybrid A* extends the search to continuous headings so that the path respects a minimum turn radius, but it still says nothing about speed, thrust or fuel.
  2. Numerical trajectory optimisation (direct shooting, multiple shooting, direct collocation, indirect methods). They enforce the equations of motion and produce control histories, at the price of a large nonlinear program that is only locally convergent.
  3. Acceleration and seeding techniques. Interior-point methods are very sensitive to the initial guess; exploiting sparsity and exact derivatives (algorithmic differentiation) keeps each iteration cheap.

docs.title: Research gap
docs.text:
Most published work treats path planning and trajectory optimisation separately, or reports a single speed-up number on easy cases. This project combines them into a hierarchical pipeline, evaluates it across a span of scenarios from empty airspace to NFZ-plus-waypoint missions, and reports where it helps, where it does not, and what it costs.

Full bibliography: References.

docs.title: 3. Methodology
docs.text:
TL;DR

The problem is non-convex and the solver only converges locally, so the formulation was grown one block at a time, validating each stage before enabling the next.

docs.title: Why not solve it in one shot?
docs.text:
A realistic 6-DoF mission becomes an NLP with thousands of variables. Three properties decide whether IPOPT succeeds:

  • Scaling. Mass in tonnes, deflections in fractions of a radian, positions in kilometres. Without non-dimensionalisation the barrier sub-problem is ill-conditioned.
  • Initial guess. A guess that violates many constraints sends the solver on a long detour through infeasibility, often to a non-physical local minimum (negative thrust, bank reversals).
  • Sparsity and exact derivatives. A dense finite-difference Jacobian makes each iteration expensive and noisy. The results in this documentation come from the first solver version (v1), which still used forward finite differences; exact derivatives arrived in a later version (see Derivatives: v1 and v2).

docs.text:

docs.title: Validation along four axes
docs.text:
Every scenario is solved with both formulations (UF and FC), for minimum time and minimum fuel. Each solution is checked on four redundant axes:

  1. Trajectory inspection: ground track and altitude profile against the expected qualitative signature.
  2. Constraint satisfaction: worst-case normalised margin per constraint and collocation defect (‖Δ‖∞ ≤ 1e-4).
  3. Time vs fuel trade-off: min-time against min-fuel on the same model.
  4. Regularisation impact: every run repeated with smoothness penalties on and off.

docs.title: Warm-start assessment
docs.text:
The warm-start chain is compared against a cold start (straight line, constant speed, zero attitude) on convergence, IPOPT iterations and wall-clock time broken down by stage (14. Warm-start benchmark). Seed quality (collocation defect of each guess) and sensitivity to the number of nodes are illustrated with the generic aircraft of the public code (Worked examples).

A deliberate choice

The full chain is not the fastest option in every single scenario; on easy geometries a leaner seed can save a few iterations. It is the default because it is the only configuration that converges in every scenario.

docs.title: 4. Design decisions
docs.text:
TL;DR

Hybrid A* + inverse dynamics → UF collocation NLP → FC collocation NLP, solved with IPOPT. Each choice favours robustness and sparsity over peak speed.

Block Chosen option Main driver Path planner / warm start Hybrid A* + inverse dynamics Deterministic, obstacle-aware, kinematically feasible seed; robust over the whole mission set Optimisation method Direct trapezoidal collocation + IPOPT Sparse NLP, friendly to warm starts and to imperfect guesses; standard for 6-DoF aerospace problems Dynamic model UF → FC hierarchy Fast, well-conditioned UF; FC adds fidelity and inherits a near-feasible iterate Cost function Bolza form (time + fuel + regularisation) Smooth Pareto sweep; regularisation removes control chatter, at a measurable cost in optimality for the 6-DoF model (13)

docs.title: Alternatives considered and left out
docs.text:
• Direct single shooting. Small NLP, but sensitive to initial guesses and unstable dynamics; path constraints are awkward.
  • Indirect (adjoint) methods. Elegant optimality structure (see Appendix) but fragile for constrained, high-dimensional problems. Used as a scaffold for understanding, not as the solver.
  • Reeds–Shepp paths. Not applicable: the aircraft cannot fly backwards.

docs.title: Why the hierarchy
docs.text:
The point-mass model solves quickly and robustly, even with NFZs. Its solution is then lifted into the 14-state rigid-body space analytically, so the expensive FC stage starts close to feasibility.

docs.title: 5. From optimal control to nonlinear programming
docs.text:
TL;DR

We want the control history that minimises a cost subject to the aircraft's equations of motion and operational limits. Discretising it turns an infinite-dimensional problem into a large but sparse NLP.

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text: A trajectory is a curve in time. An optimiser cannot search over all curves, so we sample it at a finite number of points and ask the solver to find the best values at those points, while forcing the physics to hold between neighbouring points.

docs.title: The continuous problem (Bolza form)
docs.text:
With state \(x(t)\) (position, velocity, attitude, mass…) and control \(u(t)\) (thrust, surface deflections…):

\[ \min_{u(t),\,t_f}\; J = \underbrace{\Phi(x(t_f),t_f)}_{\text{Mayer}} + \int_{t_0}^{t_f} \underbrace{L(x,u,t)}_{\text{Lagrange}}\,dt \]

subject to

\[ \dot x = f(x,u,t),\qquad x(t_0)=x_0,\qquad \Psi(x(t_f),t_f)=0,\qquad h_{\min}\le h(x,u,t)\le h_{\max}. \]
  • Mayer term: cost of the final instant, e.g. total flight time \(t_f\).
  • Lagrange term: running cost, e.g. propulsive power integrated over the flight (fuel).

docs.title: Three ways to discretise
docs.text:
Method What is discretised Strength Weakness Single shooting Controls only; states by forward integration Tiny NLP Sensitive to guesses; hard path constraints Multiple shooting Controls and states at interval boundaries Limits error growth More machinery Direct collocation Controls and states at all nodes; dynamics as algebraic constraints Robust to poor guesses, sparse, handles path constraints well Large NLP, needs a sparse solver

The decision vector then stacks everything: \(z=[t_f,\,x_0,\dots,x_{N-1},\,u_0,\dots,u_{N-1}]\).

docs.title: What the NLP solver sees
docs.text:
Equality constraints \(g(z)=0\) (dynamics defects, boundary conditions) and inequalities \(h(z)\le 0\) (terrain, NFZ, envelope). The Lagrangian

\[ \mathcal L(z,\lambda, u)=F(z)+\lambda^ op g(z)+ u^ op h(z) \]

and the KKT conditions (primal feasibility, dual feasibility \( u\ge0\), complementary slackness \( u_j h_j=0\), stationarity \( abla_z\mathcal L=0\)) characterise a local optimum. IPOPT replaces the inequalities by a logarithmic barrier and drives the barrier parameter \(\mu o0\):

\[ \mathcal L_\mu = F(z)-\mu\sum_j\ln s_j+\lambda^ op g(z)+ u^ op ig(h(z)+s ig). \]

Each iteration solves a Newton system on the KKT matrix

\[ egin{bmatrix} W_k+\Sigma_k & A_k^ op\ A_k & 0\end{bmatrix} egin{bmatrix}\Delta z\ \Delta\lambda\end{bmatrix}=- egin{bmatrix}r_{dual}\ r_{primal}\end{bmatrix} \]

which is extremely sparse because each node only couples with its neighbour. A sparse direct factorisation (MA57 / MUMPS) therefore costs roughly \(O(N)\) per iteration. A filter line-search certifies global progress without hand-tuned penalty parameters.

docs.title: 6. Uncoupled formulation (UF): point-mass dynamics
docs.text:
TL;DR

Treat the aircraft as a point mass in wind axes. The lift coefficient \(C_L\) is a direct control, so no attitude dynamics are integrated. 9 states, 3 controls, \(12N+1\) variables.

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text: The short-period and roll modes of a fixed-wing aircraft settle in a few tenths of a second, whereas a trajectory evolves over tens of seconds. The optimiser can therefore request a lift level and bank angle and assume the inner attitude loop tracks them instantly (time-scale separation). The price is that the result is not directly a set of surface commands.

docs.title: Variables
docs.text:
\[ z=[x,y,z,V,\mu,\gamma,\xi,m,C]^\top,\qquad u=[T,\,C_L,\,p]^\top,\qquad t_f\ \text{free}. \]

Position is in NED, \(V\) is airspeed, \(\mu\) the bank angle, \(\gamma\) the flight-path angle, \(\xi\) the heading, \(m\) the mass and \(C\) the battery charge (electric aircraft only).

docs.title: Equations of motion
docs.text:
\[ \begin{aligned} \dot x&=V\cos\gamma\cos\xi, &\dot y&=V\cos\gamma\sin\xi, &\dot z&=-V\sin\gamma,\\ \dot V&=\frac{T-D-mg\sin\gamma}{m}, &\dot\gamma&=\frac{L\cos\mu-mg\cos\gamma}{mV}, &\dot\xi&=\frac{L\sin\mu}{mV\cos\gamma},\\ \dot\mu&=p, &\dot m&=-\frac{c_{sfc}\,P}{3.6\times10^{6}}, &P&=\frac{TV}{\eta_p}. \end{aligned} \]

Aerodynamics: \(L=\tfrac12\rho V^2 S\,C_L\), \(D=\tfrac12\rho V^2 S\,C_D\) with a parabolic polar \(C_D=C_{D_0}+kC_L^2\) and an ISA atmosphere.

docs.title: What each equation means
docs.text:
• \(\dot V\): thrust accelerates, drag and the weight component along the path oppose.
  • \(\dot\gamma\): the vertical component of lift bends the path against gravity.
  • \(\dot\xi\): the horizontal component of lift turns the aircraft; without sideforce, a bank is the only way to turn.

docs.title: How it is implemented
docs.text:
function f_UF(state, control):          # evaluated at every collocation node
    rho  <- ISA(altitude = -z)
    L, D <- dynamic_pressure * S * (C_L, C_D0 + k*C_L^2)
    return [kinematics(V, gamma, xi),
            (T - D - m*g*sin(gamma))/m,
            (L*cos(mu) - m*g*cos(gamma))/(m*V),
            L*sin(mu)/(m*V*cos(gamma)),
            p,
            -c_sfc * (T*V/eta_p) / 3.6e6]

docs.title: 7. Full-control formulation (FC): 6-DoF rigid body
docs.text:
TL;DR

Newton–Euler equations in body axes with wind, aerodynamic angles and stability derivatives. 14 states, 4 physical controls \([T,\delta_e,\delta_a,\delta_r]\), \(18N+1\) variables. Every control is an actuator command an autopilot can execute.

docs.title: The coupling dilemma
docs.text: Aerodynamic forces depend on the incidence angles \(\alpha,\beta\), which are functions of the body velocities \((u,v,w)\), which are in turn driven by those same forces. UF breaks the loop by making \(C_L\) a free control; FC resolves it node by node in a fixed evaluation order.

docs.title: Variables
docs.text: \[ z=[x_e,y_e,z_e,m,u,v,w,\phi,\theta,\psi,p,q,r,C]^\top,\qquad u=[T,\delta_e,\delta_a,\delta_r]^\top. \]

docs.title: Evaluation order at each node
docs.text:
1. Build the NED→body rotation from the Euler angles.
  2. Rotate the wind into body axes; wind-relative velocity \((u_r,v_r,w_r)\) and airspeed \(V_a\).
  3. Aerodynamic angles: \(\alpha=\operatorname{atan2}(w_r,u_r)\), \(\beta=\arcsin(v_r/V_a)\).
  4. Coefficients \([C_L,C_D,C_Y,C_l,C_m,C_n]\) from linear stability derivatives.
  5. Forces and moments in wind axes from dynamic pressure, span and chord.
  6. Rotate to body axes; add the thrust pitching moment \(T\,d_{Tz}\).
  7. Translational dynamics: \(\dot V_b=\tfrac1m F-\omega\times V_b\).
  8. Rotational dynamics: \(I\dot\omega=M-\omega\times(I\omega)\), including the cross-inertia \(I_{xz}\).
  9. Euler-angle kinematics (singular at \(\theta\to\pm90^\circ\); not reached in normal flight).
  10. Position kinematics and mass/energy evolution.
function f_FC(state, control, wind):
    R            <- rotation_NED_to_body(phi, theta, psi)
    Vrel         <- (u, v, w) - R * wind
    alpha, beta  <- incidence_angles(Vrel)
    coeffs       <- stability_derivatives(alpha, beta, rates, control)
    F_body, M_body <- rotate_wind_to_body(coeffs, alpha, beta) + thrust_terms
    return [position_rates, mass_rate,
            F_body/m - cross(omega, V_body),
            solve(I, M_body - cross(omega, I*omega)),
            euler_rates(phi, theta, p, q, r)]

docs.title: UF vs FC at a glance
docs.text:
UF FC States / controls 9 / 3 14 / 4 Decision variables \(12N+1\) \(18N+1\) Lift \(C_L\) is a control From \(\alpha\), \(\delta_e\) and derivatives Output Path + quasi-steady lift Path + actuator commands Typical use Fast planning, warm start Fidelity, autopilot-ready output

The aerodynamic coefficients and mass data of the reference airframe are listed in the MSN012 appendix.

docs.title: 8. Transcription: trapezoidal collocation and scaling
docs.text:
TL;DR

Split the horizon into \(N-1\) equal intervals, replace the ODE by one algebraic defect per interval, and scale every residual to order one.

docs.title: Defects
docs.text:
With \(\Delta t=t_f/(N-1)\) and nodes \(k=0,\dots,N-1\):

\[ \Delta_k = x_{k+1}-x_k-\frac{\Delta t}{2}\Big[f(x_k,u_k)+f(x_{k+1},u_{k+1})\Big]=0,\quad k=0,\dots,N-2. \]

The scheme is second order in \(\Delta t\). Because \(t_f\) is a decision variable, the same NLP template expresses minimum-time and minimum-fuel problems.

docs.title: Decision vector and sparsity
docs.text:
Formulation States Controls Variables Equality block UF 9 3 \(1+12N\) \(9(N-1)\) FC 14 4 \(1+18N\) \(14(N-1)\)

Ordering variables as all states, then all controls gives a block-banded Jacobian: defect rows couple only adjacent nodes, and node-wise constraints (terrain, envelope) are block-diagonal.

docs.title: Residual normalisation
docs.text:
Rows mix metres, newtons and radians; left alone, the Jacobian is badly conditioned and IPOPT stalls. Every residual is divided by a reference scale:

\[ \tilde r = \operatorname{diag}(s_{ref})^{-1} r . \] Quantity Reference scale Position \(L_{ref}\) (mission distance) Velocity \(V_{ref}\) (cruise speed / \(V_{NE}\)) Euler angles active limit (\(\phi_{max}\), \(\theta_{max}\)), \(2\pi\) for yaw Body rates \(2V_{ref}/b\) (roll, yaw), \(2V_{ref}/\bar c\) (pitch) Controls \(T_{max}\), \(\delta_{max}\) Mass initial mass Final time \(L_{ref}/V_{ref}\)

docs.title: How it is implemented
docs.text:
function assemble_NLP(model, mission, N):
    z       <- symbolic variables [t_f, X(N), U(N)]
    g, h    <- [], []
    for k in 0 .. N-2:
        g += normalise(defect(model.f, z, k))
    g += boundary_conditions(z, mission)
    h += domain_constraints(z, mission)       # DEM, NFZ, geofence, waypoints
    h += performance_constraints(z, model)    # stall, power, V_NE, rates...
    return NLP(cost(z), g, h, sparsity = block_banded)

← Previous · Next: Constraints →

docs.title: 9. Constraint architecture
docs.text:
TL;DR

Four layers: environment, dynamics (defects), boundaries, and performance envelope. All are normalised, and all but the defects act node-wise.

docs.title: 1. Domain and environment
docs.text:
• Terrain (DEM). Bilinear interpolation of a raster elevation model gives a differentiable surface. \(z_i\ge h_{DEM}(x_i,y_i)+\epsilon_{DEM}\), with \(\epsilon_{DEM}=5\) m (absorbs the 500 m DEM resolution and between-node excursions).
  • No-fly zones. Extruded polygon prisms between \(z^{min}_j\) and \(z^{max}_j\). One signed-distance inequality per polygon face, \(d_{ij\ell}\ge\epsilon_{NFZ}=25\) m, active only inside the zone's vertical extent.
  • Geofence. Same machinery with reversed sign: stay inside the authorised polygon (margin 5 m).
  • Waypoints. To avoid if/else logic that would break a gradient-based solver, each waypoint introduces an arc-length slack \(s_{wp,k}\ge0\) and three coupled conditions (position within tolerance, attitude, speed). If a waypoint cannot be met exactly, the solver returns a minimum-violation solution rather than declaring infeasibility.

docs.title: 2. Dynamics
docs.text: The \(N-1\) collocation defects (page 8).

docs.title: 3. Boundary conditions
docs.text: Initial state fixed to the current telemetry; final position and attitude enforced as equalities (speed and mass optionally).

docs.title: 4. Performance envelope
docs.text:
Constraint UF (point mass) FC (rigid body) Anti-stall \(V/V_{stall}(h,m)\ge1\) \(V_{aer}/V_{stall}\ge1\) (wind-relative) Power available \(TV/(\eta_pP_{max}(h))\le1\) \(T\,U_r/(\eta_pP_{max}(h))\le1\) Structural \(V\le V_{NE}\) \(\lVert V_b\rVert/V_{NE}\le1\) \(C_L\) limits box bound on control nonlinear in \(\alpha,\delta_e\) Minimum altitude \(-z\ge h_{min}\) \(-z\ge h_{min}\) Actuators n/a \(\lvert\delta_{e,a,r}\rvert\le\delta_{max}\) Rates \(\lvert p\rvert\le p_{max}\) \(\lvert p,q,r\rvert\le(\cdot)_{max}\)

with \(V_{stall}=\sqrt{2mg/(\rho S_wC_{L,max})}\).

docs.title: How it is implemented
docs.text:
for each node i:
    h += -(z_i) - dem.interpolate(x_i, y_i) - eps_dem          # <= 0
    for zone in nfz:
        for face in zone.faces:
            h += eps_nfz - signed_distance(x_i, y_i, face)     # <= 0, gated by altitude band
    h += 1 - V_i / stall_speed(h_i, m_i)

docs.title: 10. Cost function: time, fuel and smoothness
docs.text:
TL;DR

One Bolza cost with a dial \(\alpha\in[0,1]\) from minimum time to minimum fuel, plus a small quadratic penalty on control increments that removes numerical chatter.

docs.title: Time–fuel trade-off
docs.text:
\[ J = (1-\alpha)\,w_{t_f}\,t_f+\alpha\sum_{k=0}^{N-2}\bar T_k\,\bar V_k\,\Delta t+J_{pen} \]
  • First term (Mayer): flight time, like a race.
  • Second term (Lagrange): propulsive power \(T\cdot V\) integrated over the flight, a proxy for fuel.
\(\alpha\) Objective Behaviour 0 Minimum time Thrust at the limit, tightest turns, high speed 1 Minimum fuel Speed near best \(L/D\), gentle climb and cruise in between Pareto front Compromise

UF uses the scalar airspeed in \(T\cdot V\); FC uses the norm of the body velocity \(\lVert V_b\rVert\) (equal in the no-wind validation).

docs.title: Why a regularisation term is needed
docs.text:
Two artefacts of direct collocation motivate \(J_{pen}\):

  1. Jacobian noise (v1 solver). With the finite-difference derivatives of the version used for the published results, the error floors near \(10^{-6}\); the KKT residual oscillates and IPOPT cannot certify convergence. A quadratic term shifts the gradient locally and smooths the search direction. With exact derivatives (later version, see Derivatives: v1 and v2) this reason disappears.
  2. Control chatter. The continuous problem has no rate limit, so the optimum may flip controls between bounds at adjacent nodes (bang-bang): pulse-like elevator, saw-tooth thrust that passes collocation but cannot be flown.
\[ J^{FC}_{pen}=\beta_c\sum_{k}\Big[w_{\Delta T}\Delta T_k^2+\sum_{s\in\{e,a,r\}}w_{\Delta\delta_s}\Delta\delta_{s,k}^2\Big]+\beta_s\sum_k\Big[w_{\Delta\phi}\Delta\phi_k^2+w_{\Delta\theta}\Delta\theta_k^2\Big] \]

(UF penalises \(\Delta T,\Delta C_L,\Delta p\) and \(\Delta\gamma,\Delta\mu\).) The rudder term prevents the solver from settling on uncoordinated flight.

docs.title: Weight selection
docs.text:
Start from zero and raise each weight in geometric steps until (i) total variation \(TV(u)=\sum_k|\Delta u_k|\) drops by about an order of magnitude and (ii) the penalty stays below ~15 % of the total cost, to limit how far the physical optimum moves. The rule does not guarantee that it stays put: for the 6-DoF model it still shifts noticeably (13. Regularisation).

docs.title: 11. Warm-start pipeline
docs.text:
TL;DR

Hybrid A* gives a turn-radius-feasible 2D path; inverse dynamics lifts it to a full state–control guess; the UF solution is projected analytically to seed FC. Each stage cuts the work of the next one.

docs.title: Why the initial guess matters
docs.text:
An interior-point method first pushes the iterate into the interior of the feasible set. A linear-interpolation guess produces collocation defects several orders of magnitude above tolerance, and the solver spends many iterations (or fails) in a restoration phase. A good guess starts the solver near the feasible manifold.

flowchart LR
    A[Mission JSON] --> B[1 Dispatcher]
    B --> C[2a Hybrid A*]
    C --> D[2b Inverse dynamics]
    D -->|ws.uncoupled| E[3 UF NLP]
    E -->|fine_UF| F[4 FC NLP]
    F -->|fine_FC| G[5-6 Export]
    E -.UF-only bypass.-> G

docs.title: Stage 2a: Hybrid A*
docs.text:
Searches the plane \((x,y,\psi)\) on an occupancy grid (25–50 m cells) that contains the NFZs. Nodes expand along unicycle arcs with \(R\in\{-R_{min},\infty,+R_{min}\}\) where

\[ R_{min}=\frac{V_{cruise}^2}{g\tan\phi_{active}} . \]

Cost \(f=g+h\), with \(h\) the maximum of the Euclidean distance and the Dubins lower bound (shortest bounded-curvature path, one of LSL, LSR, RSL, RSR, LRL, RLR). Both are admissible, so the maximum is too.

function hybrid_astar(start, goal, grid, R_min):
    open <- priority_queue{start};  closed <- {}
    while open not empty:
        n <- open.pop_min(f = g + max(euclid(n,goal), dubins(n,goal,R_min)))
        if near(n, goal): return reconstruct(n)
        for R in (-R_min, inf, +R_min):
            child <- integrate_arc(n, R, ds)           # closed form
            if blocked(grid, child) or cell(child) in closed: continue
            g_child <- g(n) + ds + turn_switch_penalty
            open.push(child)
        closed.add(cell(n))

docs.title: Stage 2b: Inverse dynamics
docs.text:
1. Resample the path to \(N\) arc-length nodes; \(\Delta t=L/(V_0(N-1))\) (constant speed).
  2. Heading and flight-path angle by finite differences.
  3. Coordinated turn: \(\phi=\arctan(V_0\dot\chi/g)\), \(q=\dot\gamma\), \(r=\dot\chi\cos\gamma\), \(p=\dot\phi-r\tan\gamma\); clamp to rate limits.
  4. Per node, a Newton trim solve gives \(T,\delta_e,(u,v,w)\) satisfying the 6-DoF force and moment balance.
  5. Integrate the mass forward.
function inverse_dynamics(path, V0, N):
    r      <- resample_by_arclength(path, N)
    chi, gamma <- finite_differences(r)
    phi, p, q, r_rate <- coordinated_turn(V0, chi, gamma);  clamp_to_limits()
    for k in 0 .. N-1:
        T[k], de[k], uvw[k] <- newton_trim(phi[k], gamma[k], rates[k], m[k])
        m[k+1] <- m[k] - fuel_burn(T[k], V0) * dt
    return state_control_guess

Nodes are trimmed independently, so the result is not optimal, but its defect is typically 2–3 orders of magnitude below a linear guess.

docs.title: Stage 4: UF → FC projection
docs.text: From \((V,\mu,\gamma,\xi)\) the angle of attack follows from the equilibrium lift coefficient \(C_{L,eq}=2mg/(\rho V^2S_w)\) and the linearised lift curve, giving \(\theta=\gamma+\alpha\). Then \((\phi,\theta,\psi)=(\mu,\theta,\xi)\); body velocities by the aerodynamic-to-body rotation; rates from the coordinated-turn relations; elevator from longitudinal trim.

docs.text:
Stages 5–6 compress the fine trajectory geometrically (cone / line-of-sight algorithm) and write JSON for the autopilot.

docs.title: 12. Validation results
docs.text:
TL;DR

Four reference scenarios in empty airspace isolate longitudinal and lateral behaviour. Every converged solution is checked a posteriori for dynamic consistency, constraint margins, UF–FC agreement and time–fuel behaviour.

docs.title: Scenarios
docs.text:
A \(2\times2\) factorial design (straight vs. 180° turn; level vs. +200 m climb), no wind, with DEM, NFZ, geofence and waypoints deactivated so that only the physics is tested.

ID Geometry ΔAlt [m] Distance [km] SC-00 Straight, level 0 3.35 SC-01 Straight, climb +200 3.36 SC-02 180° turn, level 0 4.09 SC-03 Climb + 180° turn +200 4.10

Each is solved with UF and FC, for minimum time (\(\alpha=0\)) and minimum fuel (\(\alpha=1\)).

docs.title: Acceptance metrics
docs.text: Metric Criterion Maximum normalised defect \(\lVert\Delta\rVert_\infty\le10^{-4}\), computed from the converged vector, outside the solver Constraint margins every inequality satisfies \(h_j(z)\le0\) at every node UF–FC consistency trajectories within a spatial tolerance scaled by reference length and node count Min-time vs. min-fuel qualitatively expected signatures (see below) Regularisation impact see page 13

docs.title: What the two objectives look like
docs.text:
• Minimum time: the solution saturates the propulsive envelope (maximum thrust, high speed, turns at the load-factor limit).
  • Minimum fuel: speed settles near the best-\(L/D\) condition with gentle climb and cruise.
Point-mass (UF) result for the level 180° turn (SC-02), minimum time. Rigid-body (FC) dashboard for the combined climb-and-turn (SC-03), minimum fuel.

docs.title: Minimum time against minimum fuel
docs.text:
The same scenario solved at both ends of the cost dial shows the expected trade. The minimum-fuel solution flies slightly longer and spends less energy, with lower mean thrust and gentler bank.

SC-03 (climb and turn), point-mass (left) and 6-DoF (right). For FC, minimum fuel takes 2.2 % longer and uses 9.5 % less energy, 12.4 % less mean thrust and 14.2 % less peak bank than minimum time.

docs.title: Constraint margins
docs.text:
Every converged solution is checked outside the solver against every bound and path constraint. A negative margin means satisfied; zero means active.

Point-mass model, all four scenarios, minimum time (top) and minimum fuel (bottom). Nothing is violated. In minimum time the power limit is active, as expected when the solver uses all the available propulsion; in minimum fuel the lower speed bound comes close.

6-DoF model, same layout.

Scope of this page

docs.title: 13. Effect of the smoothness regularisation
docs.text:
TL;DR

The penalties remove control chatter and make trajectories flyable, but they are not free: for the 6-DoF model they shift the optimum noticeably.

docs.title: Experiment
docs.text:
Each scenario was solved twice, with the production gates \(\beta_c=\beta_s=1\) and with the ablation \(\beta_c=\beta_s=0\), keeping the warm start and IPOPT settings identical.

FC, SC-03, minimum time. Without penalties (dashed) bank and pitch jump abruptly; with penalties (solid) they evolve smoothly.

Ground track of the same case. The two runs reach the same goal along visibly different paths.

docs.text:
Model Metric With reg. No reg. Δ [%] UF Flight time [s] 66.15 66.66 +0.77 UF Energy [J] 1.72e7 1.70e7 −1.16 UF Mean thrust [N] 4964 4844 −2.43 FC Flight time [s] 54.81 66.50 +21.3 FC Energy [J] 1.98e7 1.71e7 −13.6 FC Mean thrust [N] 5712 4819 −15.6

(Δ is as reported in the thesis table.)

docs.title: Reading the results honestly
docs.text:
• UF is barely affected: a few percent at most.
  • FC shows a much larger change in flight time and energy. The unregularised solver converges to a different time horizon with nearly the same path length (3355.8 m vs 3355.5 m). Getting a smooth optimum is harder with the full rigid-body model and often leaves it more suboptimal.
  • Total variation of the controls drops sharply on every axis, and collocation defects stay below tolerance in both cases. The unregularised runs are not "wrong" in the mathematical sense; they are just not flyable.
  • Most of the penalty mass sits on \(w_{\Delta\delta_e}\) and \(w_{\Delta T}\) in FC, and on \(w_{\Delta C_L}\) in UF: exactly the channels that oscillate most without regularisation.

docs.title: 14. Warm-start benchmark
docs.text:
TL;DR

Cold start fails the point-mass solver in every NFZ/waypoint-only scenario. The full pipeline converges 8/8, and the 6-DoF stage runs 1.2–4.4× faster than a direct seed, with the largest gain in the hardest scenario. The 6-DoF stage still misses the 4 s real-time target.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Eight scenarios × two objectives (min-fuel, min-time), two repetitions (times are means; iterations come from the fastest repetition).

Scenario Family 1–4 empty airspace 5–6 NFZ only 7 waypoints only 8 NFZ + waypoints

Two independent comparisons:

  • UF — value of the warm start. Hybrid A* + inverse dynamics (WS) against a linear-interpolation guess (No-WS).
  • FC — value of the intermediate UF stage. WS→UF→FC (full chain) against WS→FC (seed FC directly from inverse dynamics).

A run counts as feasible only if the final stage returns Solve_Succeeded / Solved_To_Acceptable_Level, produces a trajectory, and stays within the wall-clock budget (40 s).

Timing conventions

  • Times are end to end. For WS→UF→FC they include Hybrid A*, inverse dynamics, the UF solve and the FC solve. For WS→FC they include Hybrid A*, inverse dynamics and the FC solve. The comparison is therefore like for like.
  • All runs use the v1 solver, with finite-difference Jacobians (see Derivatives: v1 and v2). The absolute times overstate what the later exact-derivative version needs; the relative comparisons are what this page is about.

docs.title: UF: robustness, not always speed
docs.text:
min-fuel min-time No-WS UF converges 5/8 5/8 WS UF converges 8/8 8/8 Failing No-WS cases scenarios 5, 6, 7 (restoration failed / infeasible) same WS faster than No-WS (converged pairs) 3/5 1/5

WS UF times are 0.5–3.0 s, within the 4 s target. In easy empty-airspace cases the warm start can be slightly slower in total, because the Hybrid A* and inverse-dynamics time (40–220 ms and 2–25 ms) is added; the benefit shows where the cold start struggles: it fails outright in scenarios 5–7.

The warm start also changes which optimum the solver finds, not only how fast it gets there:

  • In scenarios 5–7 the cold-start runs end with exactly 4000.0 kg, the initial mass. They burned no fuel, so they are not physical trajectories, only the point where the solver stopped.
  • In scenario 8, where both converge, the warm-started UF reaches a better local optimum. In minimum time it flies 101.5 s against 109.5 s. In minimum fuel it ends with 3998.38 kg against 3998.26 kg, which is 0.12 kg less fuel.

  • Scenario 8 (NFZ + waypoints): 4.4× (min-fuel) and 3.8× (min-time); 111–118 iterations for the direct seed against 79–82 with the full chain.
  • Scenario 7: only the full chain converges.
  • The two pipelines end at nearly the same solution: trajectory deviation 3.3–4.5 %, end mass differences ≤ 0.1 kg.

docs.title: Limitations visible in the data
docs.text:
• FC does not meet 4 s. Total FC pipeline time with warm start is 4.5–12.9 s on this hardware; only UF (0.5–3.0 s) meets the target.
  • The full chain does not always use fewer iterations: in some scenarios WS→FC needs fewer IPOPT iterations but each is far more expensive, so wall-clock still favours the full chain.
  • Without warm start, scenario 5–7 UF trajectories also deviate 50–100 % from the warm-start ones, i.e. the cold solver was not finding the same optimum.
  • Only 8 scenarios, 2 repetitions each, one machine. These results show the mechanism, not a statistical guarantee.

docs.title: 15. Conclusions
docs.text:
TL;DR

A hierarchical warm start makes a 6-DoF trajectory optimiser robust (8/8 scenarios converge, against 5/8 from a cold start) and faster (1.2–4.4× for the 6-DoF stage) without degrading the optimum. Only the point-mass layer met the 4 s real-time target with the solver version benchmarked here (v1, finite-difference derivatives).

docs.title: What was delivered
docs.text:
An end-to-end pipeline for 3D minimum-time and minimum-fuel trajectory planning of a fixed-wing aircraft (climb, cruise, descent), with:

  • a point-mass (UF) and a 6-DoF rigid-body (FC) formulation,
  • trapezoidal direct collocation solved with IPOPT, with residual normalisation,
  • terrain, NFZ, geofence, waypoint and flight-envelope constraints,
  • a Bolza cost with a time–fuel parameter and smoothness regularisation,
  • a Hybrid A* → inverse dynamics → UF → FC warm-start chain,
  • an external validation suite and a warm-start benchmark,
  • a restricted public edition of the formulation, with a generic aircraft and runnable design examples (Code).

docs.title: What the evidence supports
docs.text:
1. A cold start is not viable for constrained missions. UF fails in 3 of 8 scenarios. Where it "stops", the trajectories are not physical: no fuel is burned.
  2. The full chain converged in every tested scenario. It made the 6-DoF stage up to 4.4× faster, and one scenario was solved only with it. Both pipelines reach practically the same optimum (3.3–4.5 % trajectory deviation, ≤ 0.1 kg end-mass difference), and in scenario 8 the warm start found a better UF optimum.
  3. Regularisation makes controls flyable at a measurable cost in optimality. The cost is much larger for FC than for UF.
  4. Derivatives matter as much as the initial guess. The published timings use finite-difference Jacobians, whose cost grows as O(N²); exact derivatives scale as O(N). The later solver version uses them (Derivatives: v1 and v2).

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Real-time target met only by UF in these numbers. FC takes 4.5–12.9 s with a warm start using the v1 solver. Exact derivatives are now implemented, and the first measurements show the UF stage about 3× faster, but the full benchmark has not been repeated with them.
  • Open-loop trajectories only; no disturbance rejection.
  • Deterministic wind only; single aircraft.
  • Aerodynamic model limited to one airframe.
  • Benchmark limited to 8 scenarios and 2 repetitions on one machine.
  • Local optimality only: IPOPT does not certify global optima.

docs.title: Future work
docs.text:
1. Re-run the full benchmark with the exact-derivative version, to verify the < 4 s target for FC and how the gain propagates through the warm-start and FC stages.
  2. Closed-loop integration with an MPC layer that uses the offline trajectory as its reference.
  3. Stochastic wind and chance-constrained NFZ/altitude constraints.
  4. Multi-aircraft coordination with shared airspace.
  5. A data-driven aerodynamic surrogate trained on flight-test data.

docs.title: Appendix: indirect (adjoint) method
docs.text:
TL;DR

The indirect route derives optimality conditions analytically (Hamiltonian, costates) before discretising. It was used to understand the problem structure, not to build the solver.

docs.title: Outline
docs.text:
For the OCP of page 5, introduce costates \(\lambda(t)\) and the Hamiltonian

\[ H(x,u,\lambda)=L(x,u)+\lambda^\top f(x,u). \]

Necessary conditions: \(\dot\lambda=-\partial H/\partial x\), \(\ \partial H/\partial u=0\) (or minimisation of \(H\) over admissible \(u\)), plus transversality at \(t_f\). Inequality path constraints are handled by multipliers or, as explored in the thesis, by an Uzawa-type iteration.

docs.title: Direct vs. indirect
docs.text:
Direct (used) Indirect Idea Discretise, then optimise Optimise, then discretise Initial guess Tolerant Needs costate guess (non-intuitive) Path constraints Natural Hard (switching structure) Insight Numerical Analytical structure

For point-mass fixed-fuel dynamics, closed-form regimes (constant-speed cruise, equilibrium turn) served as quasi-stationary references to detect non-physical local minima in early solver runs.

Back to home

docs.title: Appendix: coordinate frames
docs.text:
TL;DR

Missions arrive as geodetic coordinates (WGS-84); the optimiser works in a local NED frame; output goes back to geodetic for the autopilot.

docs.title: Frames
docs.text:
• Geodetic: latitude \(\varphi\), longitude \(\lambda\), ellipsoidal height \(h\) on the WGS-84 ellipsoid.
  • ECEF: Earth-centred Earth-fixed Cartesian \((X,Y,Z)\).
  • NED: local North–East–Down at a reference point; altitude is \(-z\).

docs.title: Chain
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    G[Geodetic<br/>lat, lon, h] --> E[ECEF] --> N[NED<br/>reference point]
    N --> E2[ECEF] --> G2[Geodetic<br/>autopilot output]

Geodetic to ECEF, with \(N(\varphi)=a/\sqrt{1-e^2\sin^2\varphi}\):

\[ \begin{aligned} X&=(N+h)\cos\varphi\cos\lambda,\\ Y&=(N+h)\cos\varphi\sin\lambda,\\ Z&=\big(N(1-e^2)+h\big)\sin\varphi . \end{aligned} \]

ECEF displacement from the reference point is rotated into NED with the local rotation built from \(\varphi_0,\lambda_0\). For long horizontal legs an altitude curvature correction compensates for the flat-earth assumption of the local frame.

Details: thesis, Annex 4.

docs.title: Derivatives: finite differences (v1) and exact derivatives (v2)
docs.text:
TL;DR

Every number in the Results chapters comes from v1 of the solver, which built the constraint Jacobian and the cost gradient by forward finite differences. A later version (v2) computes them exactly by automatic differentiation. Preliminary measurements reported in the thesis conclusions show the point-mass (UF) stage about 3× faster. The public code reproduces the mechanism: on the generic aircraft, an analytic sparse Jacobian is 57–487× cheaper to build than a finite-difference one, and the gap grows with the number of nodes.

docs.title: Why it matters for an interior-point solver
docs.text:
At every iteration IPOPT needs the gradient of the cost and the Jacobian of all constraints.

Forward differences (v1) Exact derivatives (v2) Cost of one Jacobian one constraint evaluation per decision variable: O(n) evaluations of an O(N) function, so O(N²) one sweep through the expression graph that respects sparsity: O(N) Accuracy truncation and round-off, error floor ≈ 1e-6 exact to machine precision Effect on convergence noisy KKT residual near the optimum, so the solver struggles to certify convergence clean Newton steps

The noise floor of v1 is one of the two reasons the smoothness regularisation was introduced (see 10. Cost function). With exact derivatives that reason disappears, and the regularisation is only needed against control chatter.

docs.title: What the published results therefore mean
docs.text:
• The relative conclusions hold for both versions: the warm start's robustness (8/8 against 5/8 convergence) and the advantage of the intermediate UF stage. They come from the quality of the initial guess, not from how the derivatives are computed.
  • The absolute times (FC 4.5–12.9 s) are v1 times. They overstate what v2 needs. The first v2 measurements give about 3× on the UF stage; the full benchmark has not been repeated with v2, so the < 4 s real-time target for FC is still unverified.

docs.title: The mechanism, reproduced with the public code
docs.text:
Use case UC-04 of the public code builds the trapezoidal-collocation NLP of the point-mass model for a generic UAV. It then times the defect Jacobian built both ways:

N variables analytic [ms] forward differences [ms] ratio max relative difference 25 276 0.098 5.5 57× 6.5e-11 50 551 0.180 20.7 115× 8.1e-11 100 1101 0.377 113 299× 8.8e-11 200 2201 0.654 319 487× 7.7e-11

Left: Jacobian cost against the number of nodes. Finite differences grow quadratically, the sparse analytic Jacobian linearly. Right: seed quality (see Worked examples in the Code section).

These are the costs of the Jacobian alone on a small model. The full-solver speed-up of v2 is smaller (about 3× on the UF stage in the first measurements), because the factorisation of the KKT matrix and the function evaluations stay the same. The direction and the scaling are the point.

docs.title: Code: public edition
docs.text:
TL;DR

code/ is a self-contained C++17 implementation of the thesis's formulation block: a generic aircraft described in JSON, the point-mass (UF) and 6-DoF (FC) models, the trapezoidal collocation of the optimal-control problem with an analytic sparse Jacobian, and its constraints and cost. It also includes a Hybrid A* planner and L1 path following for missions with no-fly zones and waypoints. Seven runnable use cases cover the aircraft's design charts, four typical design scenarios and four constrained missions. The optimiser and the remaining production features (terrain, geofences, the optimisation stages of the warm-start chain) are not included.

A restricted, clean-room edition

The production solver was developed as a product for Singular Aircraft and stays private. This edition was rewritten from the thesis equations. It has its own structure and naming, and a generic aircraft whose coefficients come from public sources, and it deliberately stops before the optimiser.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
Requirements: CMake ≥ 3.14 and a C++17 compiler (GCC, Clang or MSVC). There are no other dependencies. Python with numpy and matplotlib is only needed for the figures.

cd code
bash run.sh          # Linux / macOS / Git Bash: build, 25 tests, 7 use cases, figures
.\run.ps1            # Windows PowerShell

Run a single case by hand, from code/:

cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release && cmake --build build
./build/ofc data/cases/uc06_design_scenarios.json
python utils/plot_results.py            # figures in output/figures/

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[data/aircraft/*.json] --> B[Aircraft<br/>validate + derive]
    C[data/cases/*.json] --> D{use case}
    B --> D
    D --> P[performance<br/>UC-01, UC-05]
    D --> T[trim<br/>UC-02]
    D --> S[RK4 simulation<br/>UC-03]
    D --> N[TrapezoidalUF<br/>UC-04]
    D --> G[guidance + autopilot<br/>UC-06, UC-07]
    D --> H[Hybrid A* planner<br/>UC-07]
    H --> G
    G --> N
    S & N & G & P --> O[output/*.csv]
    O --> F[utils/plot_results.py]
  1. Aircraft. The JSON is validated, with errors that name the field: mass budget, positive-definite inertia, static pitch stability, stall speed below V_NE. Everything derived (V_stall(h, m), CL_max, T_max, best L/D) is computed from it and never typed in. See the aircraft file format.
  2. Models. uf::rhs, uf::jacobian and fc::rhs are pure functions f(x, u, wind).
  3. Formulation. TrapezoidalUF lays out the decision vector and evaluates everything an interior-point solver needs at each iteration: defects and their Jacobian, boundary residuals, path constraints, cost and gradient. See Formulation in code.
  4. Scenarios. A common guidance law (altitude → flight-path angle, heading or path → bank) drives the UF model by dynamic inversion and the FC model through a small autopilot. The resulting flyable trajectories are then evaluated in the NLP.
  5. Missions (UC-07). Hybrid A* plans a turn-radius-feasible path around the active no-fly zones and through the waypoints. The guidance follows it with the L1 law, and the NLP checks the result against one NFZ row per node and zone.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
Included Production only (not published) Generic aircraft model, data validation, point performance Real aircraft data UF and FC dynamics, ISA atmosphere, constant wind Layered wind profiles, geodetic (WGS-84) mission frames Trapezoidal transcription, analytic UF Jacobian, cost and gradient NLP solver interface (IPOPT) and its tuning Envelope and boundary constraints; polygonal no-fly zones with altitude band and margin; waypoints with tolerance Terrain (DEM), geofences, polyhedral NFZ with strictness, waypoint attitude/speed conditions Hybrid A* planner (Dubins heuristic and analytic expansion), L1 path following; cold-start, trimmed-line and guidance-flown trajectories Inverse dynamics → UF → FC optimisation stages of the warm-start chain Trim, RK4 simulation, closed-loop scenarios, 25 tests Mission dispatcher, autopilot export, web viewer

The excluded parts are described (equations, pseudocode and results) in the Theory and Results chapters of this documentation.

docs.title: Aircraft file format
docs.text:
An aircraft is a JSON file with the groups below. Fields marked opt. may be omitted and default to 0. Angles are in degrees; the code converts them to radians. Missing or inconsistent data stop the program with a message that names the field.

Group Field Unit Meaning — name, source text identifier and data provenance mass m0_kg, m_empty_kg, fuel_max_kg kg take-off, empty and usable fuel mass (m_empty + fuel_max ≤ m0) geometry S_m2, b_m, c_mac_m m², m wing area, span, mean aerodynamic chord inertia Ixx, Iyy, Izz, Ixz (opt.) kg m² body-axis inertia (must be positive definite) propulsion P_max_W W sea-level shaft power; lapses with altitude as 1.132 σ − 0.132 (Gagg–Ferrar) eta_p – propeller efficiency, in (0, 1] sfc_kg_per_kWh kg/kWh specific fuel consumption thrust_z_offset_m (opt.) m thrust line below (+) or above (−) the CG envelope V_ne, V_cruise m/s never-exceed and cruise speed h_min_m m minimum altitude n_min, n_max g load-factor limits (must bracket 1 g) phi_max_deg, theta_*_deg, gamma_*_deg, alpha_*_deg deg attitude, flight-path and incidence limits actuators de_max_deg, da_max_deg, dr_max_deg deg surface deflection limits p_max_dps, q_max_dps, r_max_dps deg/s body-rate limits aero.lift CL0, CLa, CLq (opt.), CLde –, 1/rad lift build-up aero.drag CD0 and either k or oswald_e – polar CD = CD0 + k CL², with k = 1/(π e AR) if oswald_e is given aero.side CY0, CYb, CYp, CYr, CYda (opt.), CYdr – side force aero.roll Cl0, Clb, Clp, Clr, Clda, Cldr – rolling moment aero.pitch Cm0, Cma, Cmq, Cmde – pitching moment (Cma < 0 required) aero.yaw Cn0, Cnb, Cnp, Cnr, Cnda, Cndr – yawing moment

Rate derivatives use the non-dimensional rates p b/(2V), q c/(2V) and r b/(2V). Derivatives with respect to angles are per radian.

Never stored, always derived (see Aircraft in code/include/ofc/aircraft.hpp):

  • CL_max = CL0 + CLa · α_max
  • V_stall(h, m) = √(2mg / (ρ S CL_max))
  • P_max(h) = P_max (1.132 σ − 0.132) and T_max(V, h) = η_p P_max(h) / max(V, V_stall)
  • (L/D)max and its speed
  • R_min = V² / (g tan φ)

To use your own aircraft, copy code/data/aircraft/generic_uav.json, change the values, check them with UC-01 and UC-05, and point the case files at the new file.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
• Frames. Positions are NED (z positive down, so altitude h = −z). Body axes are x forward, y right, z down. Euler angles are 3-2-1 (ψ, θ, φ).
  • Units. SI throughout the code. Angles are radians internally; in input files they are degrees, and those keys always end in _deg.
  • Inequalities. h(z) ≤ 0 means satisfied. Every constraint is normalised by its limit, so the values are comparable across constraints.
  • Scaling. Defect rows are divided by a reference scale per state (UfScales): the mission distance for positions, V_cruise for speed, the active limits for angles, and m₀ for mass. This keeps every residual of order one, the same normalisation described in 8. Transcription.

docs.title: Decision-vector layout (TrapezoidalUF)
docs.text:
index:  0 | 1 ............................ N·NX | N·NX+1 ................ N·(NX+NU)
        tf| x_0 (NX) | x_1 | ... | x_{N-1}       | u_0 (NU) | ... | u_{N-1}

With NX = 8 and NU = 3 there are 1 + 11N variables and 8(N−1) defects. Defect row block k couples only nodes k and k+1 (plus t_f), so the Jacobian is block-banded. At N = 200 only 0.44 % of the entries are nonzero.

docs.title: Plugging in an optimiser
docs.text:
TrapezoidalUF is solver-agnostic. An interior-point solver needs exactly what it exposes:

docs.title: Worked examples and design scenarios
docs.text:
TL;DR

All seven use cases run on the generic UAV. Headline result first, then the deeper ones:

  • Missions with no-fly zones and waypoints (UC-07). Hybrid A* finds a flyable path in 0.01–2 s (machine-dependent). UF and FC fly it while staying 11–16 m outside every margin and passing within 1.1 m of each waypoint. The straight-line cold start runs 200–394 m deep into the zones.
  • The design charts give a classic envelope: V_stall 15.1 m/s, best L/D at 20.8 m/s, V_max 36.9 m/s and a service ceiling of 5.9 km.
  • The four typical scenarios (straight and level, climb, 180° turn, climb plus turn) are flown by both models. UF and FC agree to within 0.2–67 m, with the same fuel to 0.1 g.
  • The climbs are power-limited, and the least-fuel speed (22 m/s) sits next to the best-L/D speed.
  • The analytic Jacobian is 57–487× faster than forward differences, and the gap grows with N.

All numbers on this page come from bash run.sh in code/, using the case files in code/data/cases/. The figures are produced by utils/plot_results.py. Timings depend on the machine; the trends do not.

What these results are and are not

These are flyable reference trajectories produced by a guidance law, together with design charts. They are not optimal trajectories: the optimiser is not part of the public edition. The optimal solutions of the thesis (with the real aircraft) are in 12. Validation and 14. Warm-start benchmark.

docs.title: The generic aircraft
docs.text: An 11 kg, 2.9 m-span UAV. Its mass, geometry, inertia, lift, side-force and moment derivatives follow the Aerosonde-class model of Beard & McLain (2012). Its drag polar (\(C_{D0}=0.030\), \(k=0.055\)), propulsion (800 W, \(\eta_p=0.7\), SFC 0.6 kg/kWh) and envelope limits are illustrative values chosen for this example. Data file: code/data/aircraft/generic_uav.json (format).

docs.title: UC-07 — Missions with no-fly zones and waypoints
docs.text:
The headline result

These missions are the cover of the repository. The rest of this page goes deeper: from the aircraft report (UC-01) to the typical design scenarios (UC-06).

These are the same families as the thesis benchmark (14. Warm-start benchmark), scaled to the generic UAV: 25 m/s, 30° bank, and a planning radius of 143 m.

Top views of the four missions. Red: active no-fly zones, with their margin dotted. Hatched grey: a zone below the flight altitude, overflown. Dotted grey: the straight-line cold start. Black: the Hybrid A* path. Blue and red dashed: the point-mass and 6-DoF trajectories. Green diamonds: waypoints, with their tolerance circle. M-01 one NFZM-02 slalomM-03 waypointsM-04 NFZ + waypoint + climb

The planner goes round the east side of the zone. Both models keep 11 m outside the 40 m margin (the planner's own safety distance is 10 m) and arrive on the final heading.

Two zones block opposite sides of the direct route, so the path weaves between them. The clearance plot touches the margin twice, once per zone, and never crosses it.

Each waypoint is reached heading towards the next target. Both models pass within 1.1 m of each waypoint against a 40 m tolerance.

The low zone (top at 200 m) is overflown, because the flight starts at 300 m and climbs to 450 m. The planner ignores it and the direct route crosses it legitimately. The high zone A is avoided, and the waypoint and the final easterly heading are met.

How to read the results:

  • The cold start would be infeasible. The straight line between the same end points gives NFZ rows of +6 to +11 in the NLP. With a 40 m margin that means 200–394 m inside the zones, or 240–434 m past the margin. The planned and flown trajectories give −0.3 to −0.4, so they are outside every margin. This is the same reason the thesis's cold start failed in its NFZ and waypoint scenarios.
  • The planner is cheap, and the guidance holds the path. Planning takes 0.01–2 s, depending on the machine. UF and FC end with the same clearance to the metre, and it stays above the planner's safety distance, so the 0.8 bank fraction leaves enough room to track the path.
  • Mesh resolution. The flown trajectories satisfy the collocation equations to 0.14–0.55 on 80 nodes, and to 0.004–0.014 on 320 nodes. As in UC-06, the mesh must resolve the turns.
  • What is still missing for an optimum. A trajectory like this is the warm start that the thesis then hands to the UF and FC optimisation stages. That stage, the optimiser, is not part of the public edition.

docs.text:
condition: V 25.00 m/s, h 300 m, gamma 0.00 deg, mu 0.00 deg
[UF] T 9.27 N, CL 0.5274, n 1.000 g, within limits: yes
[FC] alpha 3.198 deg, theta 3.198 deg, delta_e -8.071 deg, T 9.25 N

The two models need the same thrust (9.27 N against 9.25 N), because they share the lift and drag description. The small difference is the thrust component along the flight path, \(T\cos\alpha\), in the 6-DoF trim.

docs.title: UC-03 — Open-loop simulation
docs.text:
[UF] bank 30.0 deg after 60 s, heading change 764.6 deg, altitude change 0.01 m
     expected steady turn radius 110.4 m
[FC] doublet 2.0 deg: altitude band [299.7, 300.2] m, final theta 3.15 deg
UF rolling into a 30° coordinated turn. The heading rate matches g·tanφ/V and the altitude stays constant. FC after an elevator doublet. The short-period mode is the fast α oscillation that dies out in about 1 s. The phugoid is the slow exchange between speed and altitude, with a period of about 12 s (theory: 2πV/(g√2) ≈ 11 s).

docs.title: UC-04 — The NLP an optimiser would see
docs.text:
Straight 3.1 km leg with a 100 m climb, point-mass model, trapezoidal collocation:

    N    vars defects      nnz    dens% |    |D|cold    |D|trim |  J_an[ms]  J_fd[ms]  speedup |   jac err
   25     276     192     1872     3.53 |   7.76e+00   1.65e-15 |     0.098      5.54      57x |   6.5e-11
   50     551     392     3822     1.77 |   3.80e+00   1.08e-15 |     0.180     20.69     115x |   8.1e-11
  100    1101     792     7722     0.89 |   1.88e+00   3.99e-16 |     0.377    112.74     299x |   8.8e-11
  200    2201    1592    15522     0.44 |   9.36e-01   2.65e-16 |     0.654    318.58     487x |   7.7e-11

Left: cost of one defect Jacobian. Right: seed quality of a cold start against a trimmed straight line.
  • Derivatives. Forward differences need one full evaluation of the defects per decision variable, so their cost grows as O(N²). The sparse analytic Jacobian grows as O(N). Both agree to about 1e-10. This is the mechanism behind the speed-up between the two versions of the thesis solver: the published results were computed with finite differences, and a later version uses exact derivatives.
  • Seed quality. A cold start (straight line, zero controls) violates the dynamics by O(1). A trimmed line satisfies them to machine precision. That gap is why an interior-point solver started cold spends so many iterations in restoration (see 11. Warm start).
  • Sparsity. At N = 200 only 0.44 % of the Jacobian entries are nonzero (spy plot).

Design charts of the generic UAV.

How to read the four panels:

  1. Power curves. Required power has its minimum at the best-endurance speed. It crosses the available power (dashed, falling with altitude) at the maximum level speed.
  2. Flight envelope. Level flight is possible between the stall line and the power-limited maximum speed. The band closes at the absolute ceiling (≈ 7.0 km). V_NE never limits this aircraft because power runs out first. The best-endurance and best-range speeds (min power, best L/D) rise with altitude as 1/√σ.
  3. 6-DoF trim curves. The elevator needed to trim reaches the ±25° limit below about 17 m/s. Elevator authority, not stall, sets the minimum trimmed speed (V_stall = 15.3 m/s at 300 m). A slope of δ_e against V that is negative at low speed and flattens out is the signature of a statically stable aircraft. The 6-DoF and point-mass trim thrusts coincide (black and white dashed lines).
  4. Level turns. Turn radius against bank. Dotted segments break a limit: C_L,max at 18 m/s beyond about 43° of bank, and power at 32 m/s beyond about 58°.

docs.title: UC-06 — Typical design scenarios
docs.text:
The same 2 × 2 design as the thesis's validation scenarios: straight or 180° turn, level or +200 m climb. Each is flown at 25 m/s, with 30° of bank in turns and a 7.5° climb angle, by the point-mass model (UF, dynamic inversion) and the 6-DoF model (FC, autopilot).

SC-01  Straight, climb +200 m   |  123.9  121.8   12.1 |  0.0116  0.0117 |  -0.31    0.0 |  1.5e-01  4.2e-03 | power      0.000 |     22
SC-02  180 deg turn, level      |  100.0   99.8   15.5 |  0.0056  0.0056 |   0.01   30.8 |  5.9e-01  6.9e-02 | v_ne      -0.375 |     22
SC-03  Climb +200 m and 180 deg |  104.4  101.3   66.8 |  0.0106  0.0107 |  -0.31   31.4 |  1.1e+00  1.6e-01 | power      0.000 |     22

The four design scenarios flown by the point-mass model (solid) and the 6-DoF model (dashed). SC-00 straight, levelSC-01 climb +200 mSC-02 180° turn, levelSC-03 climb + 180° turn

The baseline. Both models stay at the trim point, and UF and FC are 0.2 m apart after 3 km.

Climbing at 7.5° needs more power than is available, so the power constraint is active (h = 0.000). The two models resolve the shortfall differently. UF holds the climb angle and bleeds airspeed. FC holds attitude and gives up a little climb angle. The fuel is the same (11.6 against 11.7 g).

FC loses about 3 m entering the turn while the autopilot builds up the extra lift (n = 1.15 g), then recovers. UF has no attitude dynamics, so it holds altitude exactly. The ground tracks differ by at most 15.5 m.

The hardest case: a power-limited climb that runs through a turn. UF slows to 22.6 m/s and turns tighter. FC keeps more speed and turns wider. This is the largest UF–FC difference (66.8 m), the same kind of model gap discussed in the thesis's UF–FC consistency check.

docs.title: Speed trade-off: minimum time against minimum fuel
docs.text:
Each scenario is flown again by the point-mass model at commanded speeds from 18 to 36 m/s:

Left: fuel against flight time for each scenario as the speed changes (fast on the left; labelled points use the least fuel). Right: fuel relative to the minimum.
  • The least-fuel speed is 22 m/s in every scenario, next to the best-L/D speed (21 m/s at 300 m). Fuel per metre is proportional to drag, which is lowest at best L/D. This is the minimum-fuel signature of the thesis (\(\alpha = 1\)).
  • Flying fast costs fuel. At 36 m/s the level scenarios burn about 60 % more fuel to save about 40 % of the time. This is the curve the cost weight \(\alpha\) of the Bolza cost moves along.
  • Climbs flatten the curve. Part of the fuel goes into potential energy whatever the speed, and at high speed the climb becomes power-limited, so time stops improving.

docs.title: The scenarios inside the NLP
docs.text:
Each UF trajectory is resampled on N = 60 and 4N = 240 uniform nodes and passed to TrapezoidalUF as a candidate solution:

  • Straight and level. The defect is at round-off level (≈ 1e-8), so the trajectory is dynamically consistent.
  • Manoeuvres. On 60 nodes (about 1.7 s spacing), the roll-in and pull-up transients, which last about 1 s, are not resolved, and the defect reaches O(0.1–1). Refining to 240 nodes cuts it by 7–36×. The mesh must resolve the fastest manoeuvre in the mission. The production solver chooses N automatically from the path length, which is why.
  • Constraints. Every path constraint is satisfied (h ≤ 0). The closest to its limit are the power constraint during climbs, which is active, and V_NE in level flight.

A trajectory like this is exactly what a warm start hands to the optimiser: flyable, nearly consistent with the collocation equations, and inside the envelope.

docs.title: Formulation in code
docs.text: The equations implemented in code/, with pointers to the source files. They are the generic counterparts of chapters 6–10. The state ordering and some modelling details differ on purpose from the production solver.

docs.title: Atmosphere and propulsion: src/model/atmosphere.cpp, aircraft.cpp
docs.text:
• Atmosphere. ISA troposphere: \(T=T_0-Lh\), \(p=p_0(T/T_0)^{g/RL}\), \(\rho=p/RT\).
  • Propulsion. A constant-power propeller. The shaft power lapses with altitude following Gagg–Ferrar, \(P_{max}(h)=P_{max,0}\,(1.132\,\sigma-0.132)\), and the available thrust is \(T_{max}=\eta_p P_{max}(h)/\max(V,V_{stall})\).

docs.title: Point mass (UF): src/model/point_mass.cpp
docs.text:
State and control:

\[x=[x_N,\,y_E,\,z_D,\,V,\,\gamma,\,\chi,\,\mu,\,m]^\top,\qquad u=[T,\,C_L,\,p_\mu]^\top\] \[ \begin{aligned} \dot x_N &= V\cos\gamma\cos\chi + w_N, &\dot y_E &= V\cos\gamma\sin\chi + w_E, &\dot z_D &= -V\sin\gamma + w_D,\\ \dot V &= \frac{T-D}{m}-g\sin\gamma, &\dot\gamma &= \frac{L\cos\mu}{mV}-\frac{g\cos\gamma}{V}, &\dot\chi &= \frac{L\sin\mu}{mV\cos\gamma},\\ \dot\mu &= p_\mu, &\dot m &= -\frac{\mathrm{sfc}}{3.6\times10^6}\,\frac{TV}{\eta_p} \end{aligned} \]

with \(L=\tfrac12\rho V^2 S C_L\), \(D=\tfrac12\rho V^2 S (C_{D0}+kC_L^2)\) and ρ(h) from the ISA. The lift coefficient is a control (time-scale separation). uf::jacobian returns ∂f/∂x and ∂f/∂u in closed form. It includes dρ/dh through the altitude dependence, which a finite-difference Jacobian only captures approximately.

docs.title: Rigid body (FC): src/model/rigid_body.cpp
docs.text:
\[x=[x_N,y_E,z_D,\,u,v,w,\,\phi,\theta,\psi,\,p,q,r,\,m]^\top,\qquad u=[T,\delta_e,\delta_a,\delta_r]^\top\]

Evaluation order at each call:

  1. Compute \(R_{nb}(\phi,\theta,\psi)\), remove the NED wind in body axes, and get \(V_a\), \(\alpha=\operatorname{atan2}(w_r,u_r)\), \(\beta=\arcsin(v_r/V_a)\).
  2. Coefficients from linear stability derivatives with non-dimensional rates \(\hat p=pb/2V_a\), \(\hat q=q\bar c/2V_a\), \(\hat r=rb/2V_a\): \(C_L=C_{L0}+C_{L\alpha}\alpha+C_{Lq}\hat q+C_{L\delta_e}\delta_e\), \(C_D=C_{D0}+kC_L^2\), and \(C_Y\), \(C_l\), \(C_m\), \(C_n\) in the same way.
  3. Rotate the wind-axis forces \([-D,\,Y,\,-L]\) to body axes, then add weight and thrust (along body x).
  4. Moments: aerodynamic, plus the thrust-line offset \((0,\;z_T T,\;0)\).
  5. Integrate:
  6. \(\dot{\mathbf v}_b = \mathbf F/m - \boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf v_b\)
  7. \(I\dot{\boldsymbol\omega}=\mathbf M-\boldsymbol\omega\times I\boldsymbol\omega\) (with \(I_{xz}\), solved in closed form)
  8. the Euler-angle kinematics and \(\dot{\mathbf r}_{NED}=R_{nb}\mathbf v_b\).

docs.title: Trapezoidal collocation: src/formulation/transcription.cpp
docs.text:
\[\Delta_k=\operatorname{diag}(s_x)^{-1}\Big[x_{k+1}-x_k-\tfrac{\Delta t}{2}\big(f(x_k,u_k)+f(x_{k+1},u_{k+1})\big)\Big],\qquad \Delta t=\frac{t_f}{N-1}\]

Jacobian blocks for interval k (row-scaled by \(s_x^{-1}\)):

w.r.t. block \(x_k\) \(-I-\tfrac{\Delta t}{2}A_k\) \(x_{k+1}\) \(I-\tfrac{\Delta t}{2}A_{k+1}\) \(u_k,\;u_{k+1}\) \(-\tfrac{\Delta t}{2}B_k,\;-\tfrac{\Delta t}{2}B_{k+1}\) \(t_f\) \(-\tfrac{1}{2(N-1)}\big(f_k+f_{k+1}\big)\)

Only structurally nonzero entries of \(A\) and \(B\) are stored. The tests verify the whole Jacobian against central differences, and check that the defect of a smooth reference trajectory shrinks like \(\Delta t^3\) (second-order global accuracy).

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
Boundary. The full initial state is fixed. At the end, position and heading are fixed.

Path (per node, \(h\le0\)):

name expression stall \(1-V/V_{stall}(h,m)\) power \(TV/(\eta_p P_{max}(h))-1\) v_ne \(V/V_{NE}-1\) load_max, load_min \(n/n_{max}-1\), \((n_{min}-n)/\max(1,\lvert n_{min}\rvert)\) altitude \((h_{min}-h)/h_{min}\) bank, bank_rate \(\mu^2/\phi_{max}^2-1\), \(p_\mu^2/p_{max}^2-1\) (smooth two-sided bounds) gamma_max, gamma_min flight-path-angle limits cl_max, thrust_min \(C_L/C_{L,max}-1\), \(-T/T_{ref}\) nfz:<id> (one per zone) \((m_j-d_j(x,y))/\max(m_j,25)\) if the node's altitude is inside the zone's band, otherwise \(-1\); \(d_j\) = signed distance to the polygon, \(m_j\) = margin

docs.title: Cost: Bolza form with a time–fuel dial
docs.text:
\[J=(1-\alpha)\frac{t_f}{t_{ref}}+\alpha\,\frac{\sum_k \bar T_k\bar V_k\,\Delta t}{E_{ref}}+\frac{\beta}{N-1}\sum_k\sum_j\Big(\frac{u_{j,k+1}-u_{j,k}}{s_{u_j}}\Big)^2\]
  • α = 0 gives minimum time and α = 1 minimum propulsive energy (a fuel proxy).
  • The β term penalises control increments, which suppresses node-to-node chatter.

costGradient is analytic, and the tests check it against finite differences.

docs.title: Initial guesses
docs.text:
• coldStartGuess: a straight line at constant speed with zero controls. This is the linear-interpolation guess against which the thesis benchmarks its warm start. Its defects are O(1).

  • trimmedLineGuess: the same geometry, but each node carries the UF trim controls for the local flight-path angle, and the mass history is integrated consistently. Its defects are at machine precision.

  • scenario::fly (UC-06): a trajectory flown in closed loop by a guidance law, then resampled on the collocation nodes. It satisfies the dynamics up to the discretisation error of the mesh.

Neither straight-line guess bends around obstacles or meets a terminal heading that differs from the bearing. With a level start, the straight climbing line also violates the initial flight-path angle; UC-04 reports this as a nonzero boundary residual. Handling those cases is what the thesis's Hybrid A* → inverse-dynamics chain does, and it is not part of this edition.

docs.title: Design-scenario guidance: src/scenarios/scenario.cpp
docs.text:
Both models share one guidance law:

\[\gamma_{cmd}=\operatorname{sat}_{\gamma_{max}}\big(k_h(h_{cmd}-h)\big),\qquad \mu_{cmd}=\operatorname{sat}_{\mu_{max}}\big(k_\chi(\chi_{cmd}-\chi)\big)\]
  • UF (dynamic inversion). The point-mass equations are inverted for the controls:
  • \(C_L\) from \(L\cos\mu=m(V\dot\gamma_{des}+g\cos\gamma)\), with \(\dot\gamma_{des}=k_\gamma(\gamma_{cmd}-\gamma)\);
  • \(T=D+mg\sin\gamma+mk_V(V_{cmd}-V)\);
  • \(p_\mu=k_\mu(\mu_{cmd}-\mu)\).

Each control is clipped to \(C_{L,max}\), \(T_{max}\) and \(p_{max}\). - FC (autopilot around the wings-level trim). - Pitch: \(\theta_{cmd}=\alpha_{trim}+C_{L,trim}(n-1)/C_{L\alpha}+\gamma_{cmd}\), held with \(\delta_e=\delta_{e,trim}+k_\theta(\theta-\theta_{cmd})+k_q q\). - Roll: \(\delta_a=k_\phi(\mu_{cmd}-\phi)-k_p p\). - Turn coordination: \(\delta_r=-k_\beta\beta\). - Speed: thrust from the trim value plus climb and speed terms.

The guidance is deliberately simple. Its purpose is to produce realistic, flyable reference trajectories for the design scenarios, not to be optimal.

docs.title: Missions with no-fly zones: src/model/environment.cpp, src/planning/planner.cpp
docs.text:
No-fly zones. A zone is a simple polygon in the horizontal plane, extruded between \(h_{min}\) and \(h_{max}\), with a margin \(m\). Its signed distance \(d(x,y)\) is the distance to the nearest edge: positive outside, negative inside (crossing-number test). A zone only counts for a flight whose altitude band overlaps \([h_{min},h_{max}]\), so a low zone can be overflown.

Dubins paths. Between two poses \((x,y,\psi)\), the shortest forward path with turn radius \(R\) is one of six words: LSL, LSR, RSL, RSR, RLR, LRL. Each word is computed in closed form, and the tests check that every word ends exactly at the goal pose.

Hybrid A*. The search runs over \((x,y,\psi)\) cells (20 m, 5°).

  • Edges. Five 30 m primitives with curvature \(\{-1,-\tfrac12,0,\tfrac12,1\}/R\), so every path is flyable at the planning radius \(R=V^2/(g\tan(0.8\,\mu_{max}))\). The 0.8 leaves bank for the guidance to correct errors.
  • Cost. Length, plus a small penalty for curvature and for changes of steering.
  • Heuristic. \(\max(\text{Euclidean},\ \text{Dubins length})\). Both are admissible lower bounds, so the maximum is too.
  • Collisions. Points every 5 m must keep \(d\ge m+\) safety from every active zone.
  • Analytic expansion. Every few expansions, and whenever the goal is within \(4R\), a Dubins shot to the goal is tried. If it is collision-free it closes the search.
  • Waypoints. The mission is planned leg by leg. Each waypoint's heading points to the next target.

L1 path following. The guidance finds the nearest point of the path, searching forward only so that loops are not skipped, and aims at a point \(L_1=2.5\,V\) further along. With \(\eta\) the angle between the course and the line to that point, the commanded lateral acceleration and bank are

\[a_{cmd}=\frac{2V^2}{L_1}\sin\eta,\qquad \mu_{cmd}=\operatorname{sat}_{\mu_{max}}\big(\arctan(a_{cmd}/g)\big).\]

The same command drives the UF model (through \(p_\mu\)) and the FC autopilot (through \(\delta_a\)). Altitude is handled by the guidance law of the previous section.

docs.title: Use cases: input reference
docs.text:
Every use case is a JSON file in code/data/cases/ with a use_case field and an aircraft path. Run them from code/:

./build/ofc data/cases/uc01_aircraft_report.json [more cases ...]

Paths are relative to the working directory. The program exits with a non-zero code if a case fails (for example, a trim that does not converge). Results and their interpretation are on the Worked examples page.

docs.title: UC-01 — Aircraft report
docs.text:
{ "use_case": "UC-01", "aircraft": "data/aircraft/generic_uav.json", "altitudes_m": [0, 1000, 2000] }

The report prints the input data and the derived performance: CL_max, k, (L/D)max, and a table over altitude with ρ, V_stall, the speed for best L/D, available power, and the thrust available at V_cruise. Use it to sanity-check a new aircraft file before anything else.

docs.title: UC-02 — Trim
docs.text:
{ "use_case": "UC-02", "aircraft": "...", "flight": { "V_mps": 25, "h_m": 300, "gamma_deg": 0, "mu_deg": 0 } }
  • UF. Closed form: \(L\cos\mu=mg\cos\gamma\) and \(T=D+mg\sin\gamma\). The report also checks the trim against C_L,max, available thrust, n_max and the bank limit.
  • FC. Newton iterations on (α, δ_e, T) that zero u̇, ẇ and q̇ in straight, wings-level flight. The starting point comes from the UF trim and the linear lift and moment model.

docs.title: UC-03 — Open-loop simulation
docs.text:
{ "use_case": "UC-03", "aircraft": "...", "flight": { "V_mps": 25, "h_m": 300 },
  "duration_s": 60, "dt_s": 0.01,
  "uf": { "bank_cmd_deg": 30, "bank_gain": 1.0 },
  "fc": { "elevator_doublet_deg": 2, "doublet_start_s": 2, "doublet_width_s": 0.5 },
  "output": "output/uc03" }
  • UF. Rolls into a coordinated turn following the quasi-steady schedule (\(C_L=C_{L,level}/\cos\mu\), T = D).
  • FC. Starts from trim with the controls frozen, plus an elevator doublet.

Outputs: uf.csv and fc.csv.

docs.title: UC-04 — Transcription check
docs.text:
{ "use_case": "UC-04", "aircraft": "...",
  "mission": { "start_ned_m": [0, 0, -300], "end_ned_m": [3000, 800, -400], "speed_mps": 25,
               "gamma_start_deg": 0, "heading_end_deg": 15, "wind_ned_mps": [0, 0, 0],
               "alpha": 1.0, "beta_control": 0.01 },
  "N": [25, 50, 100, 200], "output": "output/uc04" }

gamma_start_deg and heading_end_deg are optional. For each N, the report gives:

  • the NLP size and sparsity;
  • the maximum normalised defect of a cold start and of a trimmed straight line;
  • the time per defect Jacobian, analytic against forward differences, and the relative error between them.

After the table it gives the cost, the boundary residual, a check of the cost gradient, and the worst value of every path constraint. Outputs: transcription_check.csv and sparsity_N<smallest>.csv.

docs.title: UC-05 — Design charts
docs.text:
{ "use_case": "UC-05", "aircraft": "...", "altitudes_m": [0, 1000, 2000, 4000],
  "trim_altitude_m": 300, "turn_speeds_mps": [18, 25, 32], "mass_kg": 11.0, "output": "output/uc05" }
Output Content power_curves.csv thrust power required and available against airspeed, at each altitude envelope.csv V_stall, min-power speed, best-L/D speed, max level speed and max climb rate, every 250 m up to the absolute ceiling trim_curves.csv 6-DoF trim (α, δ_e, T) and UF trim thrust against airspeed turn.csv level-turn load factor, radius, rate and power against bank, at each speed

mass_kg is optional and defaults to m₀. The report prints the service ceiling (where the climb rate drops to 0.5 m/s), the absolute ceiling, and the envelope table.

docs.title: UC-06 — Typical design scenarios
docs.text:
{ "use_case": "UC-06", "aircraft": "...", "nodes": 60,
  "speed_sweep_mps": [18, 20, 22, 24, 26, 28, 30, 32, 34, 36],
  "scenarios": [
    { "id": "SC-03", "title": "Climb +200 m and 180 deg turn",
      "h0_m": 300, "climb_m": 200, "turn_deg": 180, "turn_start_m": 800, "distance_m": 2500,
      "V_mps": 25, "bank_deg": 30, "gamma_deg": 7.5 } ],
  "output": "output/uc06" }

V_mps, bank_deg and gamma_deg are optional. They default to V_cruise, ¾ φ_max and ½ γ_max.

Each scenario is flown by both models with the same guidance (see Formulation in code). For each one, the report gives:

  • flight time and fuel for UF and FC;
  • the largest UF–FC distance at the same along-track position;
  • the FC altitude error at the end, and the maximum FC bank;
  • the collocation defect of the flown UF trajectory on N and 4N nodes;
  • the path constraint closest to its limit;
  • the speed that uses the least fuel in the sweep.

Outputs per scenario: <id>_uf.csv, <id>_fc.csv and <id>_speed_trade.csv, plus a summary.csv for all of them.

docs.title: UC-07 — Missions with no-fly zones and waypoints
docs.text:
{ "use_case": "UC-07", "aircraft": "...", "nodes": 80,
  "planner": { "cell_m": 20, "heading_bins": 72, "step_m": 30, "bank_fraction": 0.8, "safety_m": 10 },
  "missions": [
    { "id": "M-04", "title": "NFZ, waypoint, climb; low NFZ overflown",
      "h0_m": 300, "climb_m": 150, "V_mps": 25, "bank_deg": 30,
      "start": [0, 0], "start_heading_deg": 0, "end": [3300, 1500], "end_heading_deg": 90,
      "nfz": [ { "id": "A", "polygon": [[1500, 300], [2200, 300], [2200, 1150], [1500, 1150]],
                 "h_min_m": 0, "h_max_m": 1500, "margin_m": 40 } ],
      "waypoints": [ { "id": "WP1", "position": [2700, 900], "tolerance_m": 40 } ] } ],
  "output": "output/uc07" }
  • Coordinates. Positions are [north, east] in metres, and headings are in degrees from north towards east.
  • Polygons. Each polygon is a simple polygon, in any orientation.
  • Altitude band. A zone whose band does not overlap the flight's altitudes (h0_m to h0_m + climb_m) is ignored, that is, overflown.
  • Planner settings. planner sets the search grid, the primitive length, the fraction of the bank limit used for the planning radius, and an extra safety distance on top of each zone's margin.

For each mission the report gives:

  • the planner time, the turn radius and the planned length;
  • flight times for UF and FC;
  • the smallest distance to an active zone beyond its margin (≥ 0 is acceptable);
  • the largest waypoint miss distance;
  • the collocation defect on N and 4N nodes;
  • the worst NFZ row of the NLP for the flown trajectory and for a straight-line cold start (≤ 0 satisfied).

The program exits with code 2 if a path is not found or a check fails. Outputs per mission: <id>_path.csv, <id>_uf.csv, <id>_fc.csv, <id>_nfz.csv and <id>_points.csv, plus a summary.csv.
